Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Mika had been working as an electrician on a commercial job when the assault happened, finishing up late in the day after most people had already left. He was 42, a Pacific Islander man living in the United States with his partner, and he still located the event in his mind by the hour it occurred, as if the late-afternoon light itself had become dangerous. He remembered being near a doorway when the situation turned. What stayed with him were not smooth, complete memories but a handful of hard, frozen images: the door moving, the sound of it slamming or opening abruptly, a body too close to his, a sudden shift in someone's movement that told him he was not safe. Between those images there were blanks he could not fill in. He said it was like having only a few pictures from something that should have been a full scene, and the missing parts troubled him as much as the pictures he did have.

In the weeks afterward, Mika found that when the same time of day came around, his body seemed to know before he did. Late afternoon would arrive and he would feel himself becoming unreal, as though he were no longer fully in the room. If a door opened sharply at a job site or slammed somewhere in the building, he was immediately back inside those snapshots, not in the sense of a full recollection but in the way his whole attention narrowed around the sound. He began reacting to sudden movement near him as if he were about to be hit again. A coworker stepping unexpectedly around a corner, someone crossing behind him in a narrow hallway, even his partner moving quickly into the kitchen beside him could make him jolt hard. Unexpected touch was worse. If someone put a hand on his shoulder without warning, he reacted with open alarm before he could orient himself.

As an electrician, he worked in spaces where doors opened without warning and people moved around him in close quarters, often in buildings he did not know well. He began dreading unfamiliar sites because he could not quickly judge exits, sightlines, or who might come through a door behind him. He would ask to stay on jobs he already knew, or linger near areas that felt easier to scan. When he had to enter a new building, he was tense from the moment he arrived. The strain showed at work: he was more irritable, less focused, and increasingly preoccupied with where other people were in relation to him.

At home, Mika tried hard not to think about the assault. He spent long stretches on his phone, scrolling late into the night, or disappeared into games and the internet until he was exhausted enough to sleep. He drank as a way of dulling the edge of the evening, especially when the hour of the assault approached. He also began avoiding television shows, films, or news stories that might involve violence or assault; if something unexpected came on, he shut it off or left the room. These habits narrowed his life over months. His partner saw more of his bent head lit by a screen than his face, and evenings became quiet and disconnected. He was physically present but hard to reach.

When the memory did come, guilt came with it immediately. Because he could not account for every moment, he filled the gaps with self-accusation. He had come to believe the assault said something fundamental about him: that it had happened because of the kind of person he was, because he had failed some basic test that another man would have passed. He compared himself relentlessly to an imagined stronger, smarter person who would not have ended up in that situation. What frightened him most was not only the memory itself but what he took it to mean-that his future had somehow closed down at that doorway too. He described a sense that there was nothing ahead except more vigilance, more shame, more shrinking of his world.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become difficult to hide. He was avoiding unfamiliar work settings when he could, startling at coworkers' movements, and drinking more in the evenings. His partner had begun commenting on how absent he seemed and how sharply he reacted to being touched. What finally brought him in was a recent moment on a job when a door slammed behind him near the same time of day as the assault, and he felt detached from himself so suddenly that he had to step away and sit in his truck. He said he was afraid that this was who he was now-someone weak, watchful, and finished-but he was also hoping, carefully, that talking might help him understand the missing pieces and let him feel present in his own life again.
